quests.hint: What a phone does when someone is calling you.
quests.explanation: Use the past continuous for the longer background action ('was chopping') and the past simple for the interruption ('rang'). Ring is irregular: ring, rang, rung.
quests.textToSpeak: I was chopping onions when the phone ___, so I dried my hands and answered it.
quests.correctAnswer: I was chopping onions when the phone rang, so I dried my hands and answered it.
quests.contextClue: 'Was chopping' sets the scene, and a short event breaks into it.

quests.hint: An adverb used in questions about any time in your life.
quests.explanation: 'Have you ever + past participle' asks about life experience. Answers often use 'never', 'once' or 'a few times'.
quests.textToSpeak: Have you ___ been to Japan? I'm thinking of going next spring.
quests.correctAnswer: Have you ever been to Japan? I'm thinking of going next spring.
quests.contextClue: The speaker asks about experience up to now, and 'thinking of going' explains why.

quests.hint: A small helping verb that goes before 'started'.
quests.explanation: The past perfect ('had + past participle') shows the earlier of two past events: the film started first, and then we arrived.
quests.textToSpeak: By the time we reached the cinema, the film ___ started, so we missed the opening.
quests.correctAnswer: By the time we reached the cinema, the film had started, so we missed the opening.
quests.contextClue: 'By the time we reached' sets a later moment, and the film began before it.

quests.hint: A past form of 'be' that agrees with 'everyone'.
quests.explanation: Everyone, everybody, someone and nobody take singular verbs: 'everyone was', 'everybody is', even though they refer to many people.
quests.textToSpeak: Everyone ___ tired after the long hike, so we went to bed early.
quests.correctAnswer: Everyone was tired after the long hike, so we went to bed early.
quests.contextClue: 'Went to bed' places the sentence in the past, and 'everyone' is grammatically singular.

quests.hint: A present form of 'be' that goes with a plural group.
quests.explanation: 'Police' is treated as plural in English: 'the police are', not 'the police is'. For one person, say 'a police officer'.
quests.textToSpeak: The police ___ asking anyone who saw the accident to call this number.
quests.correctAnswer: The police are asking anyone who saw the accident to call this number.
quests.contextClue: 'Asking' shows an action in progress now, and 'police' takes a plural verb.

quests.hint: The parts of your body at the end of your legs, more than one.
quests.explanation: Foot has an irregular plural: foot, feet. Others follow the same pattern: man/men, woman/women, tooth/teeth.
quests.textToSpeak: My ___ hurt after walking all day in these new shoes.
quests.correctAnswer: My feet hurt after walking all day in these new shoes.
quests.contextClue: New shoes point to a body part, and 'hurt' without -s shows a plural subject.

quests.hint: A word that asks about the amount of something you can't count.
quests.explanation: Use 'how much' with uncountable nouns (sugar, water, time) and 'how many' with countable ones (people, chairs).
quests.textToSpeak: How ___ sugar do you take in your tea?
quests.correctAnswer: How much sugar do you take in your tea?
quests.contextClue: Sugar here is a quantity, not separate items.

quests.hint: A small number; it comes right after 'a'.
quests.explanation: 'A few' + plural noun means a small number: 'a few tickets'. Without 'a', 'few' sounds more negative, as in 'few people came'.
quests.textToSpeak: There are only a ___ tickets left for Saturday, so book soon.
quests.correctAnswer: There are only a few tickets left for Saturday, so book soon.
quests.contextClue: Tickets can be counted, and 'only' tells you the number is small.

quests.hint: Information about something that has recently happened.
quests.explanation: News is uncountable and takes a singular verb: 'some good news', 'the news is'. We say 'a piece of news', not 'a news'.
quests.textToSpeak: I have some good ___ for you: you got the job!
quests.correctAnswer: I have some good news for you: you got the job!
quests.contextClue: The speaker is about to share an announcement, and 'some' shows it is not counted.

quests.hint: The small word that follows 'afraid' before the thing that frightens you.
quests.explanation: Afraid is followed by 'of' + noun or -ing: 'afraid of dogs', 'afraid of flying'.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm afraid ___ dogs, so I always cross the road when I see one.
quests.correctAnswer: I'm afraid of dogs, so I always cross the road when I see one.
quests.contextClue: Crossing the road shows the fear is connected to dogs.

quests.hint: The small word that follows 'good' when you talk about a skill.
quests.explanation: 'Good at' + noun or -ing describes a skill. 'Good with' is for handling people or things, as in 'good with children'.
quests.textToSpeak: She's really good ___ remembering names; she never forgets a face.
quests.correctAnswer: She's really good at remembering names; she never forgets a face.
quests.contextClue: Remembering names is a skill, and the second half shows she is very strong.

quests.hint: It marks the starting point of something that continues until now.
quests.explanation: 'Since' is followed by a point in time or a past clause: 'since 2015', 'since we were kids'. The main clause uses the present perfect: 'we've been'.
quests.textToSpeak: We've been friends ___ we were at primary school.
quests.correctAnswer: We've been friends since we were at primary school.
quests.contextClue: 'We've been' links past to present, so the sentence needs a starting-point word.

quests.hint: After 'enjoy', use the -ing form of the verb about paying attention to sounds.
quests.explanation: Verbs like enjoy, finish, avoid and mind are followed by -ing: 'enjoy listening', not 'enjoy to listen'.
quests.textToSpeak: I enjoy ___ to music while I cook dinner.
quests.correctAnswer: I enjoy listening to music while I cook dinner.
quests.contextClue: 'Enjoy' decides the verb form, and 'music' decides the meaning.

quests.hint: A past-tense verb meaning she put forward an idea.
quests.explanation: 'Suggest' is followed by -ing or a clause, not 'to' + verb: 'suggested meeting', not 'suggested to meet'.
quests.textToSpeak: Anna ___ meeting at the café near the station, and we all agreed.
quests.correctAnswer: Anna suggested meeting at the café near the station, and we all agreed.
quests.contextClue: If everyone 'agreed', someone first proposed the plan.

quests.hint: A past-tense verb meaning it caused a reaction in me.
quests.explanation: 'Make + person + base verb' means to cause someone to do or feel something: 'made me cry', 'made her laugh'. There is no 'to' before the verb.
quests.textToSpeak: That film ___ me cry; I wasn't expecting the ending.
quests.correctAnswer: That film made me cry; I wasn't expecting the ending.
quests.contextClue: An unexpected ending is the cause, and crying is the result.

quests.hint: A reflexive pronoun for the person you are speaking to.
quests.explanation: Use a reflexive pronoun (myself, yourself, himself) when the subject and object are the same person: 'you'll hurt yourself'.
quests.textToSpeak: Be careful on those steps or you'll hurt ___.
quests.correctAnswer: Be careful on those steps or you'll hurt yourself.
quests.contextClue: The person who might get hurt is the same person who is being warned.

quests.hint: A possessive pronoun that replaces 'my pen'.
quests.explanation: Possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs) stand alone without a noun. 'My' needs a noun after it: 'my pen', but 'mine'.
quests.textToSpeak: This isn't my pen. I think ___ is the one on the desk, next to the notebook.
quests.correctAnswer: This isn't my pen. I think mine is the one on the desk, next to the notebook.
quests.contextClue: The speaker is picking out their own pen from two.

quests.hint: A subject pronoun for more than one person.
quests.explanation: After naming a plural group, we use 'they' to avoid repeating it. 'Them' is used for objects: 'thanked them'.
quests.textToSpeak: My in-laws are lovely. Last week ___ brought us a homemade cake.
quests.correctAnswer: My in-laws are lovely. Last week they brought us a homemade cake.
quests.contextClue: 'My in-laws' are the people, and the blank is the subject of 'brought'.

quests.hint: The feeling when something happens that you did not expect.
quests.explanation: Use -ed for how a person feels ('I was surprised') and -ing for what causes the feeling ('a surprising gift').
quests.textToSpeak: I was really ___ when I opened the door and found all my friends waiting with a cake.
quests.correctAnswer: I was really surprised when I opened the door and found all my friends waiting with a cake.
quests.contextClue: Not expecting anyone at the door explains the feeling.

quests.hint: An adverb that describes how to drive, with attention to danger.
quests.explanation: An adverb describes a verb, so we add -ly to the adjective: careful becomes carefully. Say 'drive carefully', not 'drive careful'.
quests.textToSpeak: Please drive ___; the roads are icy this morning.
quests.correctAnswer: Please drive carefully; the roads are icy this morning.
quests.contextClue: Icy roads call for a particular manner of driving.

quests.hint: The noun for being able to do something well.
quests.explanation: 'Ability to + verb' is the usual pattern: 'the ability to swim'. The adjective is 'able' and the noun is 'ability'.
quests.textToSpeak: His ___ to speak three languages helped him get the job.
quests.correctAnswer: His ability to speak three languages helped him get the job.
quests.contextClue: The word after the blank is 'to', which follows a noun that means being able.

quests.hint: The superlative form of 'good'.
quests.explanation: Good, better, best are irregular. We put 'the' before a superlative, and 'by far' makes it stronger.
quests.textToSpeak: This is by far the ___ pizza I've ever eaten.
quests.correctAnswer: This is by far the best pizza I've ever eaten.
quests.contextClue: 'By far the' and 'ever eaten' point to the top of a ranking.

quests.hint: The comparative form of 'close'; it means nearer.
quests.explanation: Use a comparative for two things ('closer') and a superlative for three or more ('the closest').
quests.textToSpeak: Which of the two hotels is ___ to the beach?
quests.correctAnswer: Which of the two hotels is closer to the beach?
quests.contextClue: 'Of the two' limits the choice to two things.

quests.hint: A word that follows a comparative adjective and introduces the second item.
quests.explanation: After a comparative like 'bigger' we use 'than': 'bigger than', not 'bigger that' or 'bigger from'.
quests.textToSpeak: Their new flat is bigger ___ their old one, but it's further from work.
quests.correctAnswer: Their new flat is bigger than their old one, but it's further from work.
quests.contextClue: 'Bigger' compares two flats, and 'old one' names the second.

quests.hint: A modal verb used to give advice.
quests.explanation: 'Should + base verb' gives advice: 'you should rest'. There is no 'to' after should.
quests.textToSpeak: You ___ see a doctor if the cough doesn't go away.
quests.correctAnswer: You should see a doctor if the cough doesn't go away.
quests.contextClue: The speaker recommends an action depending on a condition.

quests.hint: A modal verb showing you are almost sure something is true.
quests.explanation: 'Must be' is used for logical conclusions: 'you must be tired'. Here it expresses strong certainty, not obligation.
quests.textToSpeak: You ___ be tired after that long flight. Sit down and I'll make some tea.
quests.correctAnswer: You must be tired after that long flight. Sit down and I'll make some tea.
quests.contextClue: A long flight is the evidence that makes the speaker sure.

quests.hint: The modal verb for a promise about the future.
quests.explanation: 'Will + base verb' is used for promises and predictions about the future. In speech it is usually shortened: 'I'll be home'.
quests.textToSpeak: Don't worry about the parcel. I ___ be at home all day tomorrow.
quests.correctAnswer: Don't worry about the parcel. I will be at home all day tomorrow.
quests.contextClue: 'Tomorrow' points to the future, and the speaker is reassuring someone.

quests.hint: The past form of 'win'.
quests.explanation: In second conditionals the if-clause uses the past simple ('If I won') and the result uses would ('I'd buy'). The past tense here shows an imaginary situation, not past time.
quests.textToSpeak: If I ___ the lottery, I'd buy a house by the sea.
quests.correctAnswer: If I won the lottery, I'd buy a house by the sea.
quests.contextClue: 'I'd buy' signals an unreal situation, so the if-clause needs a past form.

quests.hint: The past participle of the verb for constructing something.
quests.explanation: This is the passive voice: 'was built' focuses on the bridge, not on who made it. Build is irregular: build, built, built.
quests.textToSpeak: This bridge was ___ in the 1950s and needs repairs now.
quests.correctAnswer: This bridge was built in the 1950s and needs repairs now.
quests.contextClue: 'In the 1950s' gives the past time, and 'was' points to a passive form.

quests.hint: A relative pronoun used for a person.
quests.explanation: Use 'who' (or 'that') for people and 'which' (or 'that') for things: 'the woman who lives upstairs'. 'Whose' shows possession.
quests.textToSpeak: The woman ___ lives upstairs plays the piano every evening.
quests.correctAnswer: The woman who lives upstairs plays the piano every evening.
quests.contextClue: The blank links 'the woman' to the description of what she does.
